parent_issue.title: Session state not persisted
parent_issue.body:
### Summary

I am trying to use state to initialise a machine learning model but the initialization script seems to run multiple times while the script is loading and the state seems not to be updated. This is a minimal script to reproduce the behaviour
```
import streamlit as st

print([k for k in st.session_state])
if "state" not in st.session_state:
    print("Reloading")
    st.session_state["state"] = 1
```

I am expecting "Reloading" to appear once, but it appears at least twice and sometimes more, depending on browser or time of day 🤔 Is that expected? If so, is there a way to disable this behaviour?

### Is this a regression?

it seems like a regression since an earlier version did not have that problem but when I tried restoring the library to that version it was producing the same error so not sure.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: `1.10.0`
- Python version: `3.8.10`
- Using pip
- OS version: Monterey 12.3.1
- Browser version:

candidate_text:
I was able to reproduce the problem, even though I am not sure exactly why there is a problem. A library that I was using to initialize some models when I was setting the state was creating a multiprocessing pool which in turn was creating an infinite loop of crashes. Minimal code to reproduce:
```
from multiprocessing import Pool
import streamlit as st

def add_one(x):
    return x+1

print([k for k in st.session_state])
if "state" not in st.session_state:
    print("Reloading")
    with Pool(8) as p:
        p.map(add_one, range(5))
    st.session_state["state"] = 1
```

This can be fixed by disabling the multiprocessing on the library end but I am wondering whats causing this on streamlit end and whether there is anything that can be done on streamlit side.

Part of the error is 
```
RuntimeError:
        An attempt has been made to start a new process before the
        current process has finished its bootstrapping phase.

        This probably means that you are not using fork to start your
        child processes and you have forgotten to use the proper idiom
        in the main module:

            if __name__ == '__main__':
                freeze_support()
                ...

        The "freeze_support()" line can be omitted if the program
        is not going to be frozen to produce an executable.
```

preceding_comments.body: Unfortunately, I'm not able to reproduce this issue :( I only get the `Reloading` print once per session. Are you able to reproduce this issue also with an app deployed on [Streamlit Cloud](https://share.streamlit.io/)?

One possibly related observation is that if there are multiple tabs of a streamlit then "Reloading" appears once per tab as you have hinted. I sometimes end up with more than one tabs if I have stopped an app and not closed the tab, rerunning sometimes (even though not always) opens a new tab.

If this is the route of the problem, I think this will never be an issue in production and is just an annoyance when developing locally and end up with more than one tabs.

I am further investigating this behaviour in our app to definitely conclude if this is the only source state is behaving non intuitively.

parent_issue.title: Unecessary warning for date_input widget with default value rewritten by session state api
parent_issue.body:
### Checklist


### Summary

I have a date_input with min, max, default value and a key for a session_state variable as well. And because of that, the streamlit is showing an annoying warning message saying that the default value was rewritten by the session_state variable.

But when I remove the default value so only the key value from session_state is used, I got an error because by default streamlit sets the value as the current date, in which is greater than the max_value I setup in the input.

So I tried in many ways to suppress this warning but I could make it. The only way I've heard was by commenting some lines of code in the streamlit source code. But I don't want to in that way for obvious reasons.

Another person had the same problem as me [in this discussion on streamlit community](https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/why-do-default-values-cause-a-session-state-warning/15485/13). Then I came here to see if anyone had already made an issue for that.

### Reproducible Code Example

[![Open in Streamlit Cloud](https://static.streamlit.io/badges/streamlit_badge_black_white.svg)](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-6167)

```Python
import streamlit as st
import datetime

min_date = datetime.date(2020,1,1)
max_date = datetime.date(2020,12,31)

if 'custom_date' not in st.session_state:
  st.session_state['custom_date'] = min_date

st.date_input('Date:', min_value=min_date, max_value=max_date, value=min_date, key='custom_date')

st.write(st.session_state['custom_date'])
```


### Steps To Reproduce

1. Create a streamlit page with the code snippet above
2. And only for the first time you open it, will show the annoying warning
3. If you remove the default value in the date_input for the warning to not show again, it will give an error as the default date will be set the current date, in which is after the max_value.

### Expected Behavior

I expected that this warning didn't show off, or even have an option on streamlit to suppress it.

### Current Behavior

The warning message:

![Screenshot from 2023-02-22 09-59-19](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/95307858/220627491-fec590b5-c8ff-4ebb-a1e9-355be3ff916e.png)

The error message when you remove the default value:

![Screenshot from 2023-02-22 09-57-58](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/95307858/220627599-7cfd891e-c87c-43db-b9f5-3d49bc9df164.png)


### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: Streamlit, version 1.18.1
- Python version: Python 3.10.6
- Operating System: Linux Pop_OS
- Browser: Firefox
- Virtual environment: None


### Additional Information

I know that in this simple example I don't even need a session state variable. I could just set a variable for the date_input and then get the data from it. But I have a real example on my work in which I NEED to use a session state variable.

### Are you willing to submit a PR?

- [ ] Yes, I am willing to submit a PR!

candidate_text:
This looks to me like a validation issue. If a key is provided, the value in that key should be used for validation instead of a default value defined by streamlit. This should just work:

```python

import datetime

min_date = datetime.date(2020,1,1)
max_date = datetime.date(2020,12,31)

if 'custom_date' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state['custom_date'] = min_date

st.date_input('Date', min_value=min_date, max_value=max_date, key='custom_date')
```

preceding_comments.body:
Hey @eduardochaves1 👋 

Here's how you can workaround the issue. Use one session state variable to hold the default value (e.g. "custom_date"), and another to assign as the widget key (e.g. "date_key"). If the widget key doesn't exist in session state, assign the default value to the former variable:

```python
import datetime
import streamlit as st

min_date = datetime.date(2020, 1, 1)
max_date = datetime.date(2020, 12, 31)

if "date_key" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state["custom_date"] = min_date

st.date_input(
    "Date:",
    min_value=min_date,
    max_value=max_date,
    value=st.session_state["custom_date"],
    key="date_key",
)

st.write(st.session_state["date_key"])
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/20672874/220635140-91511da5-f4e1-42d3-a23f-38b8059bad5c.png)

And when I try to reset the date with the session state key, this error shows up:

And it gives the same error I was talking before that the default value date_input sets (if not specified) is the device current date, in which 2023 is greater than the max_date which is 2020

I think I didn't make myself clear enough. "This should just work" was intended to mean "it doesn't actually work and I consider that to be a bug". I think your step 3 in the **Steps To Reproduce** section of your report is the right thing to do in this case, and if it worked (which it doesn't) I wouldn't care about the warning in step 2.

parent_issue.title: st.experimental_data_editor returns the EditingState class instead of a pandas dataframe when using key parameter
parent_issue.body:
### Checklist


### Summary

When creating an st.experiemental_data_editor with the key parameter filled, the object returned by st.session_state with that key is the class EditingState from the streamlit/element/data_editor.py file.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd

dt = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 2], 'b': [2, 3]})
st.experimental_data_editor(dt, key='dt')

st.write(st.session_state['dt'])
```


### Steps To Reproduce

1) streamlit run the code block above

### Expected Behavior

st.session_state['dt'] should return a pandas dataframe

### Current Behavior

st.session_state['dt'] returns the EditingState class

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.19.0
- Python version: 3.9.16
- Operating System: Windows 10 19045.2604
- Browser: Chrome
- Virtual environment: Conda


### Additional Information

_No response_

### Are you willing to submit a PR?

- [ ] Yes, I am willing to submit a PR!

preceding_comments.body:
@kwkan-dare Thanks for reporting this! This is an expected behavior in the current version. Depending on the use case, sometimes it's more useful to have the fully edited data structure and sometimes it's better to only access the actual edits. Therefore, we decided to return the edited datastructure and only keep the edits in the sessions state (see the advanced docs [here](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/advanced-features/dataframes#access-edited-data)). Another reason why we decided to do this is that it is a lot more memory efficient. If we would add the fully edited datastrucutre to the session state as well, we would need to duplicate the dataframe. But we might change this in the future if we have more users reporting this as an issue. 

Btw. the data in the session state is a TypedDict, which is basically just a dict with better typing hints.

```Python
import streamlit as st


def expanded():
```

parent_issue.title: Date_input allows you to manually enter dates outside the min/max via keyboard input
parent_issue.body:
### Checklist


### Summary

When using the date_input widget, it is possible to type in values to the widget. Doing this allows you to enter a value that is outside the min/max range provided to the widget, and this is accepted and set in the session state with no issue. If this key is used as the input to another widget with the same state, this can cause the app to error.

### Reproducible Code Example

[![Open in Streamlit Cloud](https://static.streamlit.io/badges/streamlit_badge_black_white.svg)](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-8475)

```Python
import datetime
import streamlit as st

today = datetime.datetime.now()
next_year = today.year + 1
jan_1 = datetime.date(next_year, 1, 1)
dec_31 = datetime.date(next_year, 12, 31)

d = st.date_input(
    "Select your vacation for next year",
    (jan_1, datetime.date(next_year, 1, 7)),
    jan_1,
    dec_31
)
d
```


### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the application (code based on example from docs)
2. Click into the widget, using your keyboard enter a value outside the accepted ranges (the next year)
3. See the session state has set this value and the widget continues to work.

### Expected Behavior

I would expect the widget to cap the value to the provided min max (my preference) or raise an error similar to if you set a value on initialisation that is outside the range (less preferred, and it would be nicer for a user to just have their date set to the range limits I think)

### Current Behavior

The widget writes this value to the session state and continues to work.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.33.0
- Python version: 3.11.5
- Operating System: MacOSx
- Browser: Chrome


### Additional Information

parent_issue.title: Dialog is re-executed if `st.rerun` is triggered in an `if` statement that uses the return val from an `st.button`.
parent_issue.body:
### Checklist


### Summary

In a dialog, if `st.rerun` is placed behind an `if` block, in certain cases it will cause the entire dialog to be re-run instead of immediately closing it.

This only occurs when there's a button present and it's return value is _evaluated_ in an `if` statement's conditional.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
from time import sleep
import streamlit as st

@st.dialog("Expensive operation occurring...")
def non_dismissible_dialog():
    st.write("Hang tight for a few seconds...")

    # Not strictly necessary to re-produce bug. Just makes its effects more apparent.
    with st.empty():
        for x in range(1, 4):
            st.write(f"{x}...")
            # imagine we're doing some work here.
            sleep(1)
    st.write("All Done!")
    pressed = st.button( "Yay")
    if pressed:
        st.rerun()


# Again, not strictly necessary but makes the bug more apparent by not just immediately re-invoking the dialog.
pressed = st.button("See the bug")
if pressed:
    non_dismissible_dialog()
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run app: `streamlit main.py`
2. click button to display dialog
3. Once available, click button to close dialog
4. Dialog re-runs.

### Expected Behavior

Instead of the dialog re-running, it should immediately close.

### Current Behavior

The dialog re-runs and the simulated heavy work inside of the dialog is re-executed.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.51.0
- Python version: 3.11.10
- Operating System: macOS Sonoma 14.7.6 (23H626)
- Browser: Chrome (142.0.7444.162)


### Additional Information

Our use-case involves a non-dismissible dialog where we provide user feedback during a heavy workload.

After the work is completed, we show the user the result and allow them to click a `Close` button, and the dialog re-running the workload is disruptive.

There is a work-around that can be used by placing a conditional inside of `st.session_state` like so:

```
@st.dialog("example")
def example_dialog():
    if st.session_state.get("example_early_exit_key", None) is None:
        st.session_state["example_early_exit_key"] = "example_value"
    else:
        st.session_state["example_early_exit_key"] = None
        st.rerun()

    # continue dialog execution as normal
```

I'm not sure how reliable that work-around is tho and I don't want to put it into production if avoidable.

following_comments.body:
That is a good work around! We're using a similar method: early exit if a sentinel value is present in `st.session_storage`, but the effect is the same. 

So far, its been okay.

I looked into fixing this and want to record what I found, because I think the behavior follows from the fragment execution model rather than from a defect in the `st.rerun` plumbing — and because the obvious test harness cannot exercise it.

**`AppTest` cannot reproduce it.** I built the reported flow with a body-execution counter:

```python
@st.dialog("Expensive operation")
def my_dialog():
    st.session_state.body_runs += 1
    if st.button("Close", key="inner"):
        st.rerun()

if st.button("Open", key="outer"):
    my_dialog()
```

Driving it with `AppTest`: `body_runs` goes 0 → 1 when the dialog opens, and clicking the inner button gives **delta = 0** with the dialog closed (0 dialog blocks remaining). That is the *expected* behavior, not the bug.

The reason is that `AppTest.run()` only performs full script runs and never drives a **fragment-scoped** rerun. In `lib/streamlit/testing/v1/local_script_runner.py`, `fragment_ids_this_run` is forwarded only when the runner itself emits it; clicking a widget inside a fragment via `AppTest` does not take the fragment-rerun path the real frontend uses. So the failing path is unreachable from `AppTest`, and any unit test written there would pass vacuously.

**Why the plumbing looks correct.** Tracing the pieces:

- `elements/dialog_decorator.py` wraps the dialog body in `_fragment(...)` — a dialog *is* a fragment, and its own comment documents that closing requires `st.rerun()`.
- `commands/execution_control.py` → `_new_fragment_id_queue(ctx, "app")` returns `[]`, correctly clearing the queue so the next run is a full app run.
- `runtime/fragment.py` explicitly re-raises `RerunException` / `StopException`, so the fragment wrapper is not swallowing the rerun.

**So the mechanism appears inherent.** Any widget interaction inside a fragment re-runs that fragment. In the repro the expensive work sits *before* the button, so evaluating `if pressed:` necessarily re-executes it — before `st.rerun()` is ever reached. The dialog then closes correctly on the following app run. That ordering is a direct consequence of "widget interaction re-runs its fragment", which is also why the `st.session_state` sentinel + early-exit workaround suggested above works, and why an `on_click` callback avoids it (callbacks run before the script body).

**Which makes this a design question, not a bug fix.** Genuinely changing it would mean altering fragment rerun semantics for dialogs — e.g. suppressing the fragment rerun when the interaction will immediately request an app-scoped rerun, which is not knowable before the body runs. I did not want to guess at that in shared control-flow code, so I have not opened a PR.

If maintainers decide on a direction, two things are worth settling first:

1. Whether the intended contract is "a dialog body must be re-entrant across widget interactions" (in which case this is documentation) or "a dialog closing via `st.rerun()` should not re-execute its body" (in which case it is a semantics change).
2. If the latter, `AppTest` would need the ability to drive fragment-scoped reruns, otherwise the fix cannot be regression-tested at the unit level and would need e2e coverage.

following_comments.body:
This is a **feature request** (enhancement) to make `st.session_state` (and Streamlit commands) accessible inside the deferred-download callable that was added to `st.download_button` in 1.52 (#12942). Today the callable can't read session state, which limits the deferred-download feature when the data to export is derived from state.

The root cause is architectural rather than a bug: the deferred callable is registered via `media_file_mgr.add_deferred(...)` and only executed later, on demand, when the user clicks the button. Execution happens in `DeferredFileHandler.handle` (`lib/streamlit/runtime/backend_operation_handler.py`), which runs the callable on a separate worker thread via `asyncio.to_thread(...execute_deferred, file_id)`. Because `st.session_state` and other `st.*` commands resolve through the thread-local `ScriptRunContext`, and that context is not attached to the worker thread, the callable sees a "missing ScriptRunContext" warning and can't reach session state. Supporting this would require propagating the originating session's `ScriptRunContext` (or a scoped, read-only session-state snapshot) into the deferred execution thread. As multiple commenters note, the community workaround is a closure/factory that captures the needed session-state values into locals before the button is created.

### Related Issues

- **[#5053 — [Coming soon] Deferred data for download button](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5053)**: The original feature request that led to the deferred-download callable. This issue is a direct follow-up asking to extend that same feature so the callable can access session state.
- **[#12051 — missing ScriptRunContext! in ThreadPoolExecutor](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12051)**: Same underlying limitation — code running on a separate thread loses the `ScriptRunContext`, so session state and `st.*` commands are unavailable. Resolving context propagation to worker threads would address both.

```python
# comp.py

import sys
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import streamlit as st

st_comp_get_cookies = st.components.v2.component(
    "component_bidi_drop_bug.get_cookies",
    js="""
    export default function(component){
        const { data, setTriggerValue } = component;
        console.log("Comp Instantiated: " + data._);
        // More advanced logic here
        const retObj = document.cookie;
        console.log("cookie-getter:", retObj);
        if(retObj !== undefined) setTriggerValue("get_cookies", retObj);
    }
    """,
    isolate_styles=False,
)

def _frame_gen(frame, skip=0):
    while frame:
        if frame.f_code.co_filename.startswith("/app"):
            if skip <= 0:
                yield frame
            else:
                skip -= 1
        frame = frame.f_back

_cwd = Path.cwd()

def _rm_cwd(path):
    if _cwd in Path(path).parents:
        return str(Path(path).relative_to(_cwd))
    return path

def unique_key(suffix: str = "", skip: int = 0) -> str:
    return "".join(reversed([
        f"{_rm_cwd(f.f_code.co_filename)}-{f.f_code.co_name}-{f.f_lineno};"
        for f in _frame_gen(sys._getframe(), skip + 1)
    ])) + suffix

def unique_line_time(suffix: str = "", skip: int = 0) -> str:
    return unique_key(suffix, skip + 1) + f":{int(datetime.now().timestamp())}"
```

streamlit v 1.55

I'm trying to migrate our custom js widgets from v1 component api to the non-iframe v2 api.
It seems far more powerful, and seems like it'll cut boilerplate.
In our style, we have accumulated over the years a collection of js/client side running code, that doesn't particularly need/have an html or user-interfacing component.

I think I've noticed an issue, where values are getting returned from the js frontend (as seen by console.log msgs), but the streamlit backend logs see those msgs as dropped. I'm still getting the hang of the runtime behaviors of this new component api, to figure out how to update our v1 components, so I've been trying to test it. If this is not the expected or correct usage, I'm all ears, but I'm working my best from the online docs + repo src implementation. 

This is our current design / usage analysis of the v2 api:
- We declare/write a st.components.v2.component(...) object in a helper file, that will not be modified, with a unique name
- The js string includes all helper functions, and an `export default function(component: FrontendRendererArgs)`
- This default function is the per-widget-instantiation, and only run once (see below)
- It sets up callbacks or such on html elements
- If the component is called with a `key`, then all setTriggerValue and setStateValue items populate session_state
- Without an explicit `key`, setTriggerValue won't populate session_state, but the rest of the python arguments (data) are used to calculate a unique frontend key
- No two component instances therefore can have the exact same args (data)
- If the args to the component don't change, the widget object stays created, and is not re-instantiated
- If the rest of the args (data) to the component change, without a `key`, the old widget is discarded, and a new component is instantiated

Our goal is to have high-level code that uses caching & post processing of raw lower-level data call these low-level components as needed. But if the components are called, I expect them to behave consistently. 

In this particular example, the js component does (for example!!!) a failproof cookies query on instantiation and returns it via setTriggerValue.
```js
export default function (component){  component.setTriggerValue("get_cookies", document.cookie); }
```
We wrap that `st_comp_get_cookies: st.components.v2.component` in a helper function.
```python
def get_raw_cookies():
    obj = st_comp_get_cookies(data={"_": unique_line_time()})
```
If we feed `data` a value that's unique to the line (line traceback stack), the multiple calls of the widget will be unique even if fed the same other args. It would create a new component when there's a new/unique call (args or location), otherwise only instantiated once.
If we feed `data` a value that's unique in time, then every call is a new widget instance, and the js default function runs each time.

In the v1 api, when the app first loaded, the components wouldn't always respond right away. So I'd check if the returned value was empty or not.
```python
# get_raw_cookies()
if not isisntance(obj, dict) or "get_cookies" not in obj:
```

preceding_comments.body:
Thanks for the detailed report @alexcg1!

A couple of things I noticed while looking into this:

First, trigger values in the CCv2 API are only surfaced on the result object when you register a matching `on_<key>_change` callback ([docs](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/custom-components/components-v2/state-and-triggers#callback-registration)). Your code calls `st_comp_get_cookies(data=data)` without `on_get_cookies_change=...`, which means the `"get_cookies"` key won't appear in the result regardless of timing. Could you confirm whether your production code includes this callback?

Second, for your use case — reading cookies on component initialization — `setStateValue` would be a better fit than `setTriggerValue`. Trigger values are designed for discrete user interactions (clicks, form submissions) and reset to `None` after each rerun. State values persist across reruns, which is what you want for mount-time data. All the [documented examples](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/custom-components/components-v2/examples) call `setTriggerValue` from event handlers, not on mount.

I've put together a reproduction app exploring the behavior you described: https://issues.streamlit.app/?issue=gh-14710. I'm investigating this further with the team.

@gRodrigues03 — are you also calling `setTriggerValue` (or `setStateValue`) during component initialization to send cookie data back to Python? Or is your usage triggered by a user interaction? Just trying to understand if you're hitting the same pattern.

I do recognize now that two trigger-based widgets adjacent to each other would be like me writing `if st.button("1") and st.button("2"): ...`, both too ephemeral to happen at the same time.

For our use case, we do want the trigger-like behavior: the "cached" data could be stale. Per the above goals (clean/non-redundant session_state), I'm seeing the better design to be:
1. Have a session_state entry / wrapped variable accessor object; if the value is there, return cached value
2. If not there, run the component, stop until the value is returned (with merely a unique_key, not an ephemeral key?)
3. and then post-process and session_state cache the value as pleased
4. Optionally pre-load the values / queries on initial page load, to minimize logic interrupts
And whatever you do, don't depend on multiple simultaneous trigger-returned components.

setStateValue (or setting python component key) both invoke storing in session state, which shortcuts 1-4 (assuming you run the component on page load, stop if empty, and then post-access it only by session_state).
For organizing lots of data in the session_state, I've grown to create organizing structures within it, and to prune out any redundant entries or unneeded into (besides that minimizing state is always good). 
I'm looking forward to trying out the upcoming dataclass session state wrapper feature, but until then we've a lighter impl of that internally.

One good chunk of js-only code is talking to a parent frame that embeds streamlit apps in an iframe, such that the streamlit apps are modular sections of background services that can be composed. It was gnarly (and probably broken) before, so my stretch goal with this process is to have a sane execution flow.
But these queries naively implemented would litter the session state with unique keys / ids that no longer exist and are no longer needed. It's these ephemeral entries in session_state I'm trying to avoid with avoiding component python keys and setSavedValue. Perhaps I'm misunderstanding?

To circle back to actionable items, it would be nice if the component had a "blocking" ability to either do the if not value: st.stop, or to not even re-run at all, but block until any response, then return (minimizing needless reruns).
Or to update the docs that this is so. The current docs suggestion of "just supply a default" doesn't differentiate between expecting a value and cache invalidation.

This is a bug report about Components V2 (`st.components.v2.component`) dropping `setTriggerValue` (and `setStateValue`) results when the component's JavaScript runs on initialization (mount) rather than in response to user interaction. The root cause is a timing/race condition inherent in the Streamlit execution model: the Python script finishes execution before the frontend has a chance to render the component, load its JS module (async `import()`), execute the default function, and send the trigger/state value back via `updateWidgets`. This means the component always returns an empty/default result on its first script run. The problem compounds when multiple such components are used sequentially — satisfying one triggers a rerun that resets the other, making it effectively impossible for both to return values simultaneously. The issue discussion confirms this affects both `setTriggerValue` and `setStateValue` during mount-time initialization, and multiple community members have requested a "blocking" component mode that waits for the frontend JS to execute before the backend continues.

### Related Issues

- [#8041 - Restart app if component doesn't load](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8041): Describes the same fundamental problem for v1 components — components not being ready on first load and needing a workaround (rerun/retry). The reporter specifically notes that Components V2 should help fix this, but as this issue shows, the same timing problem persists.
- [#13671 - Allow bytes in a dict for custom components v2](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/13671): Related Components V2 enhancement for data serialization. Not a duplicate, but part of the same V2 API surface area being actively developed.
- [#9422 - `Streamlit.setComponentValue` doesn't return `Set` type variables](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9422): Related to data type handling in custom component return values. Different root cause but affects the same custom component value passing path.

parent_issue.title: Rerun on each new keystroke in `st.text_input`
parent_issue.body:
### Problem

I wanted to create a Streamlit application which has an input text field which immediately responds to user input, e.g. like the Google search field does. Something like this:

```py
def search_callback():
  st.write("You searched for:", st.session_state.input)


search_str = st.text_input('Search', key='input', placeholder='Life of Brian', on_input=search_callback)
```

### Solution

I couldn't find any way to achieve this with Streamlit. I think what would be necessary is a new type of `on_input` callback or similar.

Further, I think it would make sense to have a kwarg containing the current input. I would also have liked this for the `on_change` callback. As a workaround I have been using the session state instead:

```py
def search_callback():
  st.write("You searched for:", st.session_state.input)


search_str = st.text_input('Search', key='input', placeholder='Life of Brian', on_change=search_callback)
```

---

candidate_text:
## UPdate

This will be available in 1.64+ via the `live` parameter on `st.text_input` ([#16662](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16662)). `live=True` commits the value after a 250ms pause while typing (or pass a duration like `"300ms"`). Prefer wrapping the live UI in a fragment so typing doesn't rerun the rest of the app:

```python
@st.fragment
def search():
    query = st.text_input("Search", type="search", live=True)
    st.write("You searched for:", query)

search()
```

parent_issue.title: Fragment to fragment (co-fragment) communication instead of rerunning entire app
parent_issue.body:
### Checklist

- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Would be great to create a functionality for co-fragment communication directly rather than re-running the entire app. This could be streamlit's blockhain moment - no middle men (in this case the entire app).

### Why?

Re-rendering the entire app for co-fragment communication is frustration slow. Co-fragment communication would drastically increase the speed and performance of a streamlit app. 

### How?

My app looks like the below:

![fragments](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f5e0ea57-452c-4696-89c2-112ac27dd9b2)

The black outlines are fragments. The purple/pink outlines are nested fragments. I understand co-fragment communication occurs through session_state which is great but for this communication to be recognised, one must re-run the whole app. This makes the app more slow and somewhat buggy in my experience of operating my app. 

Seeing as fragments can be re-run periodically, it would be great to add the possibility to communicate between specific fragments via an action. For example, in my app image, After I input details in the "Contact Details" expander, I want to update the CV Preview fragment. But to do that, I have to re-run the entire app. Perhaps the possibility to rerun specific fragments based on some unique Id (like a key of a streamlit widget) when I say click on the submit form button in the Contact Details expander would be great. 

Just an example
```
@st.fragment(key="test_frag", keys_to_update=["frag1", "frag2"])
```

The issue with the above is for every rerun action, the `keys to update` will rerun. So perhaps, we could create a trigger command parameter.

```
@st.fragment(key="test_frag", keys_to_update=["frag1", "frag2"], trigger_keys=["form_submit_btn"])
```

We could also get fancy and connect trigger keys to keys to update:


```
@st.fragment(key="test_frag", keys_to_update=["frag1", "frag2"], trigger_keys=[{"frag1":"form_submit_btn"}])
```
